name: Persian Gulf
description: The Persian Gulf is a shallow, semi-enclosed sea between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, connected to the Gulf of Oman through the Strait of Hormuz. Its geography links evaporation-driven ocean circulation, ancient coastal landscapes, and internationally important maritime routes.

seo.title: Persian Gulf: Geography, Water Exchange and Coastal History | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand the Persian Gulf’s shallow basin, exchange through Hormuz, changing prehistoric coastline, and environmental connections.

content.heading: A shallow sea with an ocean connection
content.content:
The Persian Gulf lies between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. Its connection to the wider Indian Ocean runs through the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. These names describe connected but distinct geographic features: the strait is the narrow passage, while the Gulf of Oman is the basin beyond it. [s1][s4]

The Persian Gulf’s shallowness is fundamental to its character. NOAA’s regional oceanographic documentation gives an average depth of approximately 36 metres and describes a deeper channel toward the Iranian coast, contrasting with broader shelves on the Arabian side. A map of the shoreline therefore tells only part of the story: the underwater landscape is uneven, influencing how water moves through the basin. [s1]

content.heading: Why evaporation drives exchange
content.content:
Evaporation removes freshwater while leaving dissolved salts behind. The resulting density differences help sustain an exchange in which relatively fresher water enters through Hormuz near the surface and denser, saltier water leaves at depth. Oceanographers describe this as inverse-estuary circulation. Wind and tides modify the exchange, so the two-layer description is a useful explanation rather than a complete map of every current. [s2]

This connection matters environmentally. The Gulf is semi-enclosed, but its waters are continually exchanged with neighbouring seas. A study of desalination and basin-wide salinity published in 2022 found that overturning circulation and export through Hormuz substantially limited modelled salinity accumulation. That finding concerns the scale and assumptions of the model; it should not be treated as proof that individual discharge sites have no environmental effects. [s3]

content.heading: A coastline that changed before written history
content.content:
The present sea occupies a landscape that was profoundly altered by postglacial sea-level rise. Archaeologist Daniel Potts’s synthesis explains that, during lower sea levels, much of the basin was exposed land crossed by a river system associated with the Tigris, Euphrates, and Karun. Subsequent inundation submerged earlier landscapes. [s5]

This creates a practical limit on archaeological interpretation. Modern shores are not reliable guides to where prehistoric communities encountered the sea. An apparent absence of early coastal sites on land may partly reflect submergence, rather than an absence of human activity. Potts discusses early pottery finds on the Bushehr peninsula alongside evidence from the Arabian shore, placing Iran’s coast within a wider regional setting. [s5]

content.heading: Geography and maritime dependence
content.content:
Hormuz concentrates shipping between the Persian Gulf and the open ocean. The US Energy Information Administration’s June 2025 analysis explains that many regional oil shipments have limited alternatives, although some pipelines bypass the strait. This establishes the geographic dependence of maritime trade; its historical traffic figures do not establish operating conditions in October 2026. [s4]

The Persian Gulf is best understood through these overlapping connections: an uneven shallow basin, an evaporation-driven exchange, a submerged prehistoric landscape, and a narrow maritime outlet. Each explains a different part of its importance to Iran and its neighbours. [s1][s2][s4][s5]

name: Gulf of Oman
description: The Gulf of Oman connects the Strait of Hormuz with the Arabian Sea, forming the oceanward continuation of Iran’s southern maritime geography. Its waters receive dense outflow from the Persian Gulf and include an oxygen minimum zone studied using autonomous ocean gliders.

seo.title: Gulf of Oman: Ocean Connections and Marine Oxygen | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the Gulf of Oman’s connection to Hormuz and the Arabian Sea, its Persian Gulf water inflow, and research on oxygen-depleted waters.

content.heading: Beyond the Strait of Hormuz
content.content:
The Gulf of Oman is the oceanward link between the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. For readers following Iran’s southern coast on a map, it marks a change from the Persian Gulf’s semi-enclosed setting toward the wider Indian Ocean. Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman belong to the same maritime connection, but they are not interchangeable names. [s1]

That distinction also matters for trade. Ships leaving the Persian Gulf through Hormuz continue through the Gulf of Oman toward ocean routes. The EIA’s geographic account explains why the narrow passage concentrates movement even though the sea beyond it is more open. Geography establishes this relationship; it does not establish whether particular ports or routes are operating normally on a given date. [s1]

content.heading: Water masses cross the boundary
content.content:
The connection is physical as well as commercial. Dense, saline water formed in the Persian Gulf flows outward and influences the Gulf of Oman. A study by Iranian oceanographers combined observations with a dynamical model to investigate how this outflow spreads. It described the influence of Earth’s rotation in keeping the outflow against the Omani coast, together with extensions farther into the basin. [s2]

The study also explored how changing the properties of the source water could alter the outflow. These were modelled scenarios, not observations of inevitable future conditions. The wider lesson is that neighbouring seas cannot be understood as isolated containers: water formed under one basin’s climatic conditions can affect another basin’s underwater structure. [s2]

content.heading: An oxygen problem beneath the surface
content.content:
An oxygen minimum zone is a body of seawater with unusually low dissolved oxygen. Research published in 2018 used autonomous Seagliders and historical observations to investigate oxygen distribution in the Gulf of Oman. The researchers found oxygen depletion that was poorly represented in existing climatologies—datasets describing typical ocean conditions. [s3]

The result is more specific than saying that the entire gulf is lifeless. Oxygen varies with depth, location, and water movement. The research examined how eddies redistribute oxygen and how the proportions of oxygenated and very low-oxygen water vary spatially and seasonally. Low oxygen also changes nitrogen cycling, making the issue important beyond its immediate effects on marine animals. [s3]

Contemporary reporting on the research explains another difficulty: insecurity and piracy had restricted opportunities to collect observations. Robotic instruments helped fill that gap, but a survey cannot substitute for continuous monitoring. The 2018 findings should therefore be read as dated evidence of a serious oceanographic condition, not a measured map of oxygen throughout the gulf in 2026. [s4]

content.heading: Look below the shipping map
content.content: The Gulf of Oman is both a maritime connection and a dynamic marine environment. Surface routes show how ships pass between seas; observations below the surface reveal moving water masses and sharply differing oxygen conditions. Understanding both helps explain why a seemingly continuous stretch of blue on a map contains distinct environmental processes. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Lake Urmia
description: Lake Urmia is a hypersaline lake in northwestern Iran whose extent responds to inflow, evaporation, and water use across its closed drainage basin. Satellite records document severe contraction interrupted by temporary refilling, while surrounding wetlands support habitats distinct from the salty lake itself.

seo.title: Lake Urmia: Shrinkage, Wetlands and Restoration Evidence | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Lake Urmia’s closed-basin water balance, satellite evidence of contraction and refilling, surrounding wetlands, and restoration challenges.

content.heading: A lake without an outlet to the sea
content.content:
Lake Urmia lies in northwestern Iran. It is hypersaline—extremely salty—and belongs to a closed drainage basin. Water reaches the lake through precipitation and inflowing rivers, while evaporation removes water without carrying away its dissolved salts. Diversions upstream can therefore alter the balance even when they occur far from the shoreline. [s1][s3]

The lake’s shape makes changes in water extent uneven. US Geological Survey imagery explains that the southern basin is shallower than the northern basin, so water disappears from the south first during contraction. A photograph from one shore cannot establish conditions throughout the lake. Nor does an exposed lakebed necessarily describe the condition of every nearby wetland. [s1]

content.heading: Refilling did not end the longer decline
content.content:
Satellite evidence shows a long decline interrupted by wetter episodes. USGS describes a general reduction in surface area since 1995, followed by a pulse of water associated with rainfall in autumn 2018 and spring 2019 and seasonal snowmelt. Later imagery shows renewed contraction. [s1]

NASA’s October 2023 account compared Landsat views from 2020 and September 2023, documenting the return of extensive exposed salt flats after the earlier replenishment. Its explanation identifies agricultural water diversion, dams, drought, and other climatic pressures as relevant to the decline. The evidence supports a combined water-management and climate explanation, rather than a single-cause story. [s2]

These observations also explain why recovery claims need a time dimension. Water returning after heavy rain establishes a real hydrological improvement at that time. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that the basin can maintain an adequate water balance through subsequent dry seasons. The documented reversal after refilling is central to understanding Urmia’s restoration challenge. [s1][s2]

content.heading: The lake and its neighbouring wetlands
content.content:
Conservation here involves a mosaic of habitats. IUCN distinguishes the extremely salty lake from surrounding wetlands with different salinity conditions. These habitats support different ecological communities and should not be treated as one uniform body of water. [s3]

IUCN’s account highlights surrounding wetlands used by the endangered white-headed duck, including Hasanlu and Kani Barazan. It identifies inadequate water supply, human pressures, and pollution among threats to these habitats. Protecting birds therefore requires attention to the water conditions and management of individual wetlands as well as the main lake. [s3]

The lake is recognised as a Ramsar wetland, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, and a national park. These designations establish conservation significance; they do not demonstrate that ecological recovery has been achieved. [s3]

content.heading: Restoration needs measurable outcomes
content.content:
Agricultural water management remains part of the institutional response. FAO’s safeguards portal lists documentation dated January and September 2026 for a project addressing effective agricultural water use in Lake Urmia’s restoration. The existence of those documents establishes an active programme of work, not a measured increase in water reaching the lake. [s4]

A defensible assessment must connect interventions to sustained inflow, lake conditions, and wetland outcomes. This account does not assign a current water area or declare restoration complete: a consistent monitoring record through the editorial cutoff remains necessary.
